bill.name: United States Secret Service Reserve Fund Act of 2026 (H.R. 8058)
bill.status: Introduced in House · Mills · referred to House Judiciary on March 24, 2026
bill.analyzed: Full introduced-in-House bill (4 pages; §§1–2), with §2 as the sole substantive provision.

sourceLimits: The supplied 3,145-byte, 515-word raw source contains all substantive provisions of the introduced bill but is flattened to one line, has no page boundaries or metadata sidecar, and omits the standard enacting clause visible in the official PDF. The matching official GovInfo introduced-version PDF establishes the four-page count. The source incorporates 18 U.S.C. §3056 without reproducing the protected-person categories and supplies no baseline Secret Service appropriations, protective costs, staffing or protectee counts, lapse history, fiscal justification, implementation record, account identifier, report template, public-release requirement, or protection-performance target. The $106 million is a statutory appropriation and potential fund balance, not a forecast of obligations, outlays, or service continuity. The report goes only to named congressional committees and need only describe uses and transactions; publication and standardized fields are not required. The fixed December 31, 2026 balance snapshot and January 31, 2027 transfer deadline are not reconciled with a lapse or spending window spanning year-end, and the report trigger is potentially unclear if no amount remains to transfer. Goals below are therefore restrained inferences from the operative duties. No defensible recurring official series or public one-time resolution record follows from the text, so metrics and conditionals are empty and no series hints or stance matrices are supplied.

provisions.title: Section 2 — United States Secret Service Reserve Fund
provisions.heading: §2: $106 million reserve for protective expenses during a Secret Service appropriations lapse
provisions.quote: “for the necessary expenses of the United States Secret Service related to the protection of individuals identified in section 3056 of title 18, United States Code (including the payment of the salaries of employees who directly provide such protection), during a lapse of appropriations for the United States Secret Service.” … “There is hereby appropriated, out of money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $106,000,000 for the United States Secret Service Reserve Fund.”
provisions.context: Section 1 supplies only the short title. Section 2 establishes the reserve for necessary Secret Service expenses related to protecting people identified in 18 U.S.C. §3056, expressly including salaries of employees who directly provide that protection. The Director may, rather than must, draw from the reserve only during a lapse in appropriations for the Secret Service, beginning on the lapse date and ending when the lapse ends or 30 days after it begins, whichever is earlier. The bill appropriates $106 million from the Treasury and directs the Secretary of the Treasury to deposit the money into the reserve, but it does not require any amount to be spent. By January 31, 2027, the Director must transfer to the Treasury, for rescission, qualifying unused amounts remaining as of December 31, 2026. Within 30 calendar days after complying with that transfer requirement, the Director must submit a report on fund uses and transactions to six named House and Senate committees. The text does not extend the reserve to all Secret Service operations, guarantee uninterrupted protection, quantify the amount needed during a lapse, or require the report to be published.
goals: Make up to $106 million available for necessary Secret Service expenses related to protecting people covered by 18 U.S.C. §3056, including direct-protection salaries, during the first 30 days or shorter duration of an appropriations lapse.
Confine use of the reserve by purpose and time, return and rescind the qualifying unused balance after 2026, and report the fund's uses and transactions to the named congressional committees.

effects.text: If enacted, the bill would appropriate $106 million and require the Secretary of the Treasury to deposit it into the new reserve. That creates a fund balance available under the bill's conditions; it does not require the full amount, or any amount, to be obligated or spent.

The Director could use the reserve during a qualifying lapse only for necessary expenses related to protection under 18 U.S.C. §3056, including salaries of employees who directly provide that protection. The provision does not cover every Secret Service function or compel a draw.
Authority to use the reserve would end when the lapse ends or 30 days after the lapse begins, whichever occurs first. A lapse lasting longer than 30 days would not extend this spending window.

The Director would have to transfer qualifying unused amounts remaining as of December 31, 2026, to the Treasury by January 31, 2027, and those amounts would be rescinded. The text rescinds the balance but does not expressly abolish the fund itself or provide a replenishment mechanism.

Within 30 calendar days after compliance with the transfer requirement, the Director would have to report fund uses and transactions to the six listed committees. The bill specifies neither publication nor standardized contents beyond those broad subjects.

barriers.actor: Secret Service and Treasury financial administrators
barriers.text: Administrators would have to identify which expenses are sufficiently related to §3056 protection, which employees directly provide it, and how deposits, draws, unused amounts, transfers, and rescission are recorded, without a deposit deadline or accounting detail in the bill.
The text supplies no adequacy analysis, priority rule, or replenishment authority if eligible protective expenses exhaust the $106 million before the lapse ends or the 30-day limit is reached.

barriers.actor: Secret Service and Treasury officials applying the calendar rules
barriers.text: The bill does not explain how the December 31 balance snapshot and January 31 transfer deadline interact with an eligible lapse or use window that begins before year-end and continues afterward, or with enactment near or after either fixed date.

The report deadline runs from the date of compliance with the transfer requirement, which may be unclear when no balance remains, and the report need not be public or follow a specified format. The text therefore supplies no guaranteed public record for verifying complete implementation or protection continuity.
